description: Heat supplied to a process from a site heat system at a delivery temperature below 150 degC: hot water and low-pressure steam for washing and CIP, pasteurizing, bleaching, stock heating, evaporation, low-temperature drying; generic low-temperature direct heaters. Banded on the temperature the process needs, not on the steam grade. Cogeneration sits here too: a CHP unit is a technology that supplies this band, with electricity as a co-product (2026-09-14, reversing the separate chp end use).
note: 150 degC is roughly where commercial heat pumps stop [design doc s2; etsap_2013_002 165 degC; rtc_2023_001 heat pump < 160 degC], so this is the band where they compete. caelp_2024_001 puts 84% of food and 80% of pulp and paper indirect heat below 100 degC but only 28% of chemicals.

description: Heat supplied at 150-400 degC: medium- and high-pressure steam, thermal oil and direct heaters for distillation reboilers, digesters, stripping, polymer melting and extrusion, panel pressing, and fired heaters feeding refinery distillation. Cogeneration sits here too, as a technology supplying the band rather than an end use of its own (2026-09-14).
note: Heat pumps fall away above about 200 degC [caelp_2024_001 p.11 uses 200 degC as the practical delivery bound], leaving combustion, electric boilers and heaters, thermal storage and CHP.

description: Heat above 400 degC supplied by a fired heater or furnace that is separable from the unit doing the transformation: refinery process heaters for conversion units, generic industrial furnaces and heaters, superheated steam above 400 degC. Heat released INSIDE a sector's own process unit (kiln, blast furnace, cracker furnace, lime kiln, glass furnace) is not here; it belongs to that sector's end use.
note: NRCan records refinery furnaces at 200-700 degC (79 PJ), straddling medium and high; its bands are < 200 / 200-700 / > 700 degC and do not map onto ours.

description: Electricity generated on site with no useful heat recovered: diesel and gas gensets at off-grid mines and oil-and-gas sites, gas turbines and engines, condensing steam turbines, power plants firing by-product gases, and solar, wind and storage in site microgrids.
note: Brought into scope on the user's decision (2026-09-11), reversing design doc s1, which put power-only generation out of scope. At isolated northern mines diesel is over 80% of energy use (Energies 2026 review). The CHP/power-only boundary is heat recovery.

description: Motor-, engine- and turbine-driven pumps moving liquids and slurries around a site. Excludes pipeline pumping, which is an oil-and-gas end use.
note: EIA MECS splits machine drive into pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, materials processing and a residual; these five end uses follow that split, and the MECS residual is not carried - motor-driven equipment none of the five covers is filed under materials processing.

description: Process fans, blowers and induced- and forced-draught sets. Excludes building ventilation and mine ventilation, which are their own end uses.
note: EIA MECS splits machine drive into pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, materials processing and a residual; these five end uses follow that split, and the MECS residual is not carried - motor-driven equipment none of the five covers is filed under materials processing.

description: Compressed-air systems and the process compression that serves them. Excludes pipeline and gas-processing compression, which are oil-and-gas end uses.
note: EIA MECS splits machine drive into pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, materials processing and a residual; these five end uses follow that split, and the MECS residual is not carried - motor-driven equipment none of the five covers is filed under materials processing.

description: Conveyors, cranes, hoists, stackers and reclaimers moving solids around a site.
note: EIA MECS splits machine drive into pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, materials processing and a residual; these five end uses follow that split, and the MECS residual is not carried - motor-driven equipment none of the five covers is filed under materials processing.

description: Motor-driven size reduction, mixing, forming and separation that is NOT already counted in a sector end use - comminution, mechanical pulping, rolling and cement grinding all stay with their sector.
note: EIA MECS splits machine drive into pumps, fans, compressed air, materials handling, materials processing and a residual; these five end uses follow that split, and the MECS residual is not carried - motor-driven equipment none of the five covers is filed under materials processing.

description: Heating and ventilating plant buildings and warehouses: unit heaters, radiant tubes, make-up air units, supply and exhaust air handling, heat-recovery ventilation and building heat pumps.
note: Mine ventilation and mine air heating are a mining end use. Building ventilation was folded into space heating and space cooling on 2026-09-16.

description: Cooling and ventilating offices, control rooms and production space, including supply and exhaust air handling.
note: Building ventilation was folded into space heating and space cooling on 2026-09-16.

description: Interior and yard lighting, and its controls.
Non-road vehicles and equipment used on site: construction equipment, loaders, forklifts, yard trucks, slag and log handling, oil-and-gas field vehicles.
note: Material because construction sits in other-industry: construction is 3.1% of Canadian industrial energy, mostly off-road diesel (NRCan Trends 2017). NRCan also shows 1.3 PJ diesel in pulp and paper. Mine haulage and oil-sands truck fleets stay with their own sector end uses.

description: Capture from process streams where the CO2 is already concentrated and nitrogen-free: shifted syngas and acid-gas removal in ammonia, methanol and hydrogen plants (including upgrader hydrogen units), formation CO2 removed at gas-processing plants, fermentation CO2 at ethanol plants, pre-combustion capture on gasifiers, oxygen-blown iron routes (HIsarna, smelting reduction, syngas DRI, top-gas recycling), indirectly heated calciners, oxy-fuel flue gas. The work is drying and compression, with little or no solvent regeneration.
note: IPCC Table 11.3: 99% reduction, TRL 9, <= USD40/t, available today; footnote f calls disposal of concentrated CO2 at USD15-40/t well established. IPCC names HIsarna and syngas DRI as concentrated; smelting reduction, Corex and top-gas recycling are put here by analogy (oxygen-blown, nitrogen-free gas) and need a source. An SMR has both kinds: process CO2 from the shift is concentrated, the reformer furnace flue is dilute. CIMS books one rate for it. Integrated routes (hisarna-ccs, shaft-furnace_syngas_ccs, calciner_ccs) stay on their sector end use as technology choices; this end use is the capture service they draw on. CIMS has no capture option on ethanol fermentation CO2; its Ethanol.CCS serves only boilers. Sector and cross-sector rows named `<host>_ccs-concentrated` point here: the capture plant's cost and energy are held on this end use once and are not repeated on the host row, which carries only the host-side effects.

description: Post-combustion capture from flue gas where the CO2 is diluted in nitrogen: boilers, CHP, fired heaters, cement and lime kiln stacks, cracker furnaces, FCC regenerators, sinter strands and EAF off-gas.
note: IPCC Table 11.3: up to 90% reduction, TRL 6-7, <= USD120/t, from 2025. For cement IPCC splits the same plant two ways: calcination CO2 from an indirect calciner <= USD40/t (concentrated), fuel CO2 <= USD120/t (dilute). Direct air capture is its own end use, direct-air-capture. IPCC's term is 'diluted in nitrogen'; 'diffuse' here means the same thing. Sector and cross-sector rows named `<host>_ccs-diffuse` point here: the capture plant's cost and energy are held on this end use once and are not repeated on the host row, which carries only the host-side effects, such as the steam drawn for regeneration.

description: Capture of CO2 from ambient air by liquid-solvent or solid-sorbent processes, with compression; the CO2 goes to storage (carbon removal) or becomes a carbon feedstock for synthetic fuels and chemicals.
note: IPCC Table 11.3: up to 99% reduction, TRL 3, about USD94-232/t, available by 2030, listed as a carbon source for CoOxHy fuels and feedstocks. Kept apart from point-source capture because it serves no emitting process: it draws CO2 from air rather than a stack, is sited independently of any plant, and competes as a removal or a feedstock supply rather than as abatement on a process. The harmonized row tp-1509 stores its abatement cost as 2.0 USD/t; the IPCC cell reads about USD94-232/t, so that is an extraction error.

description: Coke ovens and the by-product plant.
note: NRCan: 16.9 PJ coke and coke-oven gas at > 700 degC.

description: Sinter plants and pellet induration at the steelworks.
note: Most Canadian pellets are made at the mine; see mining pelletizing, which uses the same technologies.

description: Reduction of iron ore: blast furnace with hot stoves, direct reduction (shaft furnace with reformer or hydrogen), smelting reduction. The routes compete to supply the same service.
note: NRCan: blast furnaces 40.7 PJ; DRI methane reformer 14.4 PJ natural gas. CIMS does not split ironmaking from steelmaking.

description: BOF and EAF (scrap and DRI charge), ladle metallurgy and ladle preheating.
note: Scrap availability bounds the EAF share; the EAF/BOF split is a technology choice within this end use.

description: Cryogenic and adsorption air separation supplying oxygen to the basic oxygen furnace, the electric arc furnace and the blast furnace, on site or over the fence.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector air-separation end use (2026-09-14): oxygen is a sector service, sized by the steel route. Small oxygen uses elsewhere - glass oxy-fuel firing, oxy-fuel capture, merchant industrial gases - are not carried as end uses.

description: Ingot, continuous, thin-slab and strip casting of liquid steel into semis.
Reheating slabs, billets and blooms to rolling temperature, and hot charging that avoids it.
note: NRCan: high-temperature furnaces 45.9 PJ (natural gas, coal, coke-oven gas) at > 700 degC.

description: Roughing and finishing stands, section, bar, rod and tube mills, tandem and reversing cold mills, acid pickling and skin pass.
note: Rolling heat comes from reheating.

description: Batch and continuous annealing, tempering, electrical-steel treatment, hot-dip galvanizing, electro-galvanizing and tin plating.
note: Zinc-bath temperature is not in held or checked sources.

description: Raw meal preparation and drying, preheater and precalciner, rotary kiln, clinker cooler.
note: NRCan: calciners 55.5 PJ at > 700 degC. Raw milling is kept here, not in machine drive, because it moves with the kiln choice.

description: Finish grinding, supplementary cementitious material preparation and blending, alternative binders.
note: Clinker ratio is decided here, which is why grinding is not folded into machine drive.

description: Lime and dolomitic lime kilns.
note: NRCan: lime calciners 10.7 PJ at > 700 degC.

description: Batch and cullet preparation, melting and refining in container, flat, fibre and specialty glass furnaces; mineral wool melting.
note: Split from melting-and-firing on 2026-09-16, following the CIMS hierarchy glass nodes: glass furnaces and ceramic kilns have different technology sets.

description: Forming, annealing lehrs, tempering and fire polishing of glass products.
note: Split from melting-and-firing on 2026-09-16: annealing and tempering are a different energy service from melting.

description: Brick, tile, sanitaryware and refractory firing in tunnel, roller and periodic kilns.
note: Split from melting-and-firing on 2026-09-16.

description: Gypsum calcining to stucco, clay and brick drying, other mineral product drying.
Olefin pyrolysis furnaces and cold-end separation.
Reforming (SMR, ATR), shift and synthesis for ammonia and methanol, including the hydrogen made on the way.
note: The reformer is the same technology as the refinery and merchant hydrogen plants; it stays here because it is integral to the ammonia or methanol plant.

description: Chlorine-caustic electrolysis, caustic evaporation, sodium chlorate cells.
note: Sodium chlorate supplies pulp bleaching, which is why it is material in Canada.

description: Polymers, aromatics (BTX), organic intermediates, hydrogen peroxide, other bulk and fine chemicals: reactors, distillation, stripping, drying, extrusion.
note: Nitric and adipic acid are a separate end use (split 2026-09-16): their N2O emissions differ in kind and are abated by N2O destruction.

description: Ammonia oxidation to nitric acid, and adipic acid made by nitric acid oxidation: the N2O-emitting processes.
note: Split from other-chemicals on 2026-09-16 under the emissions rule: N2O process emissions, abated by catalytic or thermal destruction. The CIMS hierarchy gained a nitric acid node on 2026-09-17.

description: Grain (corn, wheat) dry milling, liquefaction and cooking, fermentation, distillation and dehydration, stillage evaporation, distillers-grain drying; cellulosic ethanol.
note: Canada has about 1,900 million L/yr of ethanol nameplate capacity (CER). In the US, ethyl alcohol is 10% of chemical-sector energy (307 TBtu, DOE 2015). Fermentation CO2 is nearly pure: co2-capture-concentrated. CIMS's Ethanol.Agricultural Input (farm diesel for feedstock) is agriculture and stays out of scope.

description: Oil and fat pretreatment, transesterification, methanol recovery, glycerin refining, biodiesel distillation.
note: Canada has about 700 million L/yr of biodiesel capacity (CER). Renewable diesel (HVO) is a different product and route: see renewable-diesel-and-saf.

description: Dedicated hydrotreating (HEFA/HVO) units, including converted refineries, that make renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel from vegetable oils, tallow and used cooking oil: feed pretreatment, hydrodeoxygenation, isomerization, fractionation.
note: Moved from petroleum-refining on the user's decision (2026-09-11). Canada produced about 687 million L in 2024 and planned capacity could triple (CER). Its hydrogen demand is what separates its energy use from biodiesel's. Co-processing in existing refinery hydrotreaters stays in refining.

description: Biogas raised from anaerobic digestion or landfill and upgraded to pipeline specification, and biomass gasification to methane.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector hydrogen-and-fuel-supply end use (2026-09-14): RNG is produced for sale into the gas system, which makes it a biofuels product rather than a site service.

description: Merchant hydrogen produced for sale rather than for an on-site process: steam methane and autothermal reformers with and without capture, gasification, and grid- or dedicated-renewable electrolysis at plant scale.
note: New sector, 2026-09-14. Split from on-site production because the plant is sized by the merchant market, not by one host process, and because its emissions and its capture economics are the hydrogen sector's, not the user's.

description: Compression, pipeline transmission and distribution of hydrogen to industrial users, including booster compression, and liquefaction and trucking where there is no pipeline.
note: New sector, 2026-09-14. Distribution energy is a real cost of centralized supply and is what distinguishes it from production at the point of use.

description: Desalting, atmospheric and vacuum distillation.
note: The heaters are CIMS's separate Direct Heat service, hence 'draws' rather than 'integral'.

description: FCC, hydrocracking, coking, catalytic reforming, alkylation, isomerization, asphalt and lubes, hydrotreating and sulphur recovery. Co-processing bio-feedstock in an existing hydrotreater stays here as a feedstock choice; dedicated renewable diesel and SAF units are in biofuels.
note: NRCan: FCC catalyst regeneration burns 50.8 PJ of petroleum coke as captive combustion.

description: Hydrogen made at the refinery for hydrotreating and hydrocracking: steam methane and autothermal reformers with and without capture, petroleum-coke gasification, and electrolysis.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector hydrogen-and-fuel-supply end use (2026-09-14): a refinery hydrogen plant is sized and fuelled by the refinery. 37.6 PJ of reformer natural gas is booked as a non-energetic input.

description: Log thawing, debarking, chipping and chip screening for pulp mills.
note: Split out on 2026-09-16: debarking and chipping serve every virgin-fibre route, not only chemical pulping.

description: Kraft and semi-chemical digesting, washing, oxygen delignification and bleaching.
Thermomechanical, chemi-thermomechanical and groundwood refining, with refiner heat recovery.
note: Split from mechanical-and-recycled-pulping on 2026-09-16: refiners use several times the electricity of repulping and the technologies do not compete. The refiners are the process (rule 5), so they are no longer a link to materials-processing.

description: Recovered-paper repulping, screening, cleaning and deinking.
note: Split from mechanical-and-recycled-pulping on 2026-09-16.

description: Multiple-effect evaporators and the recovery furnace.
note: boiler_black-liquor_recovery sits on .steam in design doc s4.1; here it is the chemical-recovery service, with its steam output credited to the heat end uses.

description: Recausticizing lime kiln.
note: NRCan: 22.6 PJ natural gas and oil at > 700 degC, the mill's main direct fossil heat.

description: Stock preparation and refining, headbox and wire, press section, and sheet finishing for all grades.
note: Electricity-dominated; the dryer section is a separate end use.

service-unit-default: t water evaporated or t product
description: Dryer section (steam cans, hoods, infrared), coating dryers and market-pulp drying.
note: NRCan: dryers 7.5 PJ at 200-700 degC. CIMS paper grades stay as process steps.

description: Primary clarification, biological treatment and sludge handling on mill effluent: aeration basins, activated sludge, anaerobic reactors, clarifiers, presses and dryers.
note: Added 2026-09-15. Aeration is one of the largest single electricity loads in a kraft mill after the refiners and the paper machine, and anaerobic treatment turns part of the load into recovered biogas, so it is a real technology choice rather than generic pumping.

description: Drilling, blasting, loading, hauling and hoisting in open-pit and underground metal, coal and potash mines; solution-mining extraction.
note: NRCan diesel in mining equipment, trucks and trains: iron ore 7.6 PJ, gold and silver 17.1 PJ.

description: Primary and secondary crushing, milling and grinding, crush-and-screen.
note: The largest electricity use in metal mining; kept out of machine drive because ore hardness and grind size, not motor choice, set the energy.

description: Flotation and other separation, cleaning and washing, potash dissolution and crystallization, compaction, tailings disposal.
Potash and concentrate drying, and thermal drying of washed coal.
note: Tier is a placeholder until a source gives dryer temperatures.

description: Pellet induration at the mine.
note: NRCan: 23.4 PJ in pelletizing furnaces (13.7 PJ oil at > 700 degC). Same technologies as iron-and-steel agglomeration.

description: Underground ventilation fans, mine air heating (and cooling in deep mines).
note: Taken out of facility services because of its scale and distinct technologies. NRCan: gold and silver mine space heating 3.8 PJ below 200 degC. CIMS keeps the fan technologies in the shared machine-drive fan service; only the coal mine-air duty (`coal-mining.product.raw-product.mine-ventilation`) is a node of its own, and metal mining has none.

description: Mine dewatering, water treatment before discharge or reuse, process-water reclaim, and tailings transport, thickening and storage.
note: Added 2026-09-15. Separated from comminution and separation because the driver is the site water balance and the discharge permit, not the ore throughput, and because dewatering pumping runs whether or not the mill does.

description: Drilling rigs, completions and hydraulic fracturing, well testing and servicing.
note: Fracturing pump spreads are among the largest diesel loads in the sector; electric fleets compete.

description: Light, medium, heavy and offshore oil and conventional, tight, shale and coalbed-methane gas wells: artificial lift, field compression, heater-treaters and line heaters, wellsite dehydration, pneumatic controllers and pumps, liquids unloading, enhanced oil recovery.
note: Gas-driven pneumatics are a methane-venting service more than an energy one; CIMS models electric replacements. Field compression is a demand here; the drivers that meet it are compressor-drive-engine and compressor-drive-turbine.

description: Separation, treatment, recycling and disposal of produced and flowback water: disposal-well injection, de-oiling and softening for steam generation, evaporators and crystallizers, and recycling for makeup.
note: Added 2026-09-15. In-situ bitumen recycles most of its produced water, so the water plant is part of what sets the steam-to-oil ratio; disposal injection carries its own energy and its own regulatory constraint. Kept out of in-situ-bitumen because it also serves conventional production and fracturing.

description: Gas deliberately released to atmosphere, and the equipment that avoids, recovers or destroys it: pneumatic controllers and pumps, process and tank venting, blowdowns for maintenance, liquids unloading.
note: Split from venting-and-flaring on 2026-09-16: other source data report venting and flaring separately, and the CIMS hierarchy keeps them apart. Deliberate release: the volume is event- and equipment-driven and largely metered or estimated per event, and the abatement is equipment substitution. The enclosed combustor destroys vapours that would otherwise be vented, so release and destruction compete here. The service is really tonnes of methane; the unit is the gas disposed of on an energy basis.

description: Solution-gas and process flaring: gas burned rather than sold, and the equipment that recovers it or raises destruction efficiency.
note: Split from venting-and-flaring on 2026-09-16. The service is the gas burned, on an energy basis.

description: Unintentional leaks from valves, flanges, connectors, seals, compressor packings and storage, and the survey, monitoring and component programs that find and cut them.
note: Split from venting and flaring, 2026-09-15. Leaks scale with component count and stock age rather than with throughput, the volume is inferred from emission factors or top-down measurement rather than metered, and the abatement is a program - survey frequency, monitoring, low-emission components - not a device that competes with a vapour recovery unit. Canadian methane regulations set LDAR frequency separately from venting limits. Top-down measurement often cannot attribute observed methane between unburnt flare gas, venting and leaks; where a source does not attribute it, say so rather than splitting on an assumption.

description: SAGD, cyclic steam stimulation, solvent-assisted and hybrid thermal-solvent recovery: steam generation and injection, produced-water treatment and recycling, bitumen treating.
note: The boilers are separable, so the steam draws on the heat bands. Solvent routes compete by cutting the steam needed rather than supplying it differently. CIMS already offers electric, hydrogen and nuclear steam here.

description: Truck-and-shovel mining, ore preparation and hydrotransport, hot- or warm-water bitumen extraction, froth treatment, tailings handling.
note: The haul fleet stays here rather than in mobile-equipment, as mine haulage does in mining.

description: Upgraders that turn bitumen into synthetic crude: coking, hydrocracking, hydrotreating, sulphur recovery.
note: Same technologies as petroleum-refining conversion-and-treating. It is kept in this sector because upgraders are integrated with oil sands operations and CIMS models them in Petroleum Crude.

description: Hydrogen made at a bitumen upgrader for hydroconversion: steam methane reformers with and without capture, and gasification of asphaltenes or petroleum coke.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector hydrogen-and-fuel-supply end use (2026-09-14). Quest captures from these reformers, which is why the concentrated-stream capture row sits here.

description: Sweetening (amine), dehydration (glycol), sulphur recovery, NGL extraction and fractionation, inlet and sales compression.
note: Acid gas stripped from raw gas is concentrated CO2, the classic low-cost capture stream.

description: Gas pre-treatment, refrigeration-cycle compression and liquefaction, boil-off handling.
note: LNG Canada (Kitimat, two trains, 14 Mtpa) shipped its first cargo in 2025 (Shell). The drive choice, gas turbine or electric, is the main technology decision.

description: Compressor stations on transmission pipelines; gas-distribution systems, including line heaters at pressure let-down stations.
note: Pipeline transport emitted 8.3 Mt CO2e in 2019, mostly from compressor-station combustion (CER). Transmission and distribution leaks add 2.4 Mt, but those are emissions, not energy. The compression is a demand here; the drivers that meet it are compressor-drive-engine and compressor-drive-turbine, split by driver as the CIMS hierarchy splits them (2026-09-22).

description: Stationary diesel, gasoline and propane engines at oil and gas sites, driving pumps, generators and other field equipment: requested per well, per m3 of bitumen and by upgraders. Excludes compressor drivers and haul fleets, which have their own end uses.
note: One end use for the one CIMS node, petroleum-crude.service.field-engines (2026-09-22). Drilling, production, in-situ bitumen and upgrading reference it through draws-on instead of each claiming part of it.

description: Reciprocating compressors and their drivers, mostly natural gas engines, with electric-motor replacements, meeting field gathering, gas-processing and pipeline compression demand.
note: Split by driver as the CIMS hierarchy does, natural-gas.service.compressor-drive.engine (CIMS Direct Drive Small, 10-year life, 2026-09-22). The three compression end uses draw on it in exogenous shares. Rod packing and blowdowns are methane sources counted on venting and fugitive-emissions.

description: Centrifugal compressors and their drivers, mostly natural gas turbines, with large electric-motor replacements, meeting processing and pipeline compression demand and some field compression.
note: Split by driver as the CIMS hierarchy does, natural-gas.service.compressor-drive.turbine (CIMS Direct Drive Large, 30-year life, 2026-09-22). Turbine exhaust is the waste-heat-to-power opportunity at compressor stations.

description: Pump stations on crude, bitumen blend and refined-product pipelines, plus drag-reducing and heating where used.
note: Oil pipelines mostly use electric motors, so they emit much less than gas pipelines (CER).

description: Cooking, blanching, scalding, pasteurizing, sterilizing and retorting, evaporating and concentrating, brewing, washing and CIP.
Ovens, fryers and roasters.
note: Harmonized files ovens under process-heat-high-temp; the sources put them at 100-232 degC.

description: Spray, drum, belt and grain drying; sugar and pulp drying.
Chilling, freezing and cold storage: vapour-compression plant, ammonia and CO2 systems, spiral and blast freezers, and the cold rooms they serve.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector process-cooling-and-refrigeration end use (2026-09-14): food and beverage is where process cooling is a real energy service. Chemical-plant and gas-plant refrigeration stays inside the process end use it serves.

description: Bayer digestion, clarification, precipitation and calcination.
note: NRCan: 7.4 PJ (boiler 3.0, calciner 4.5).

description: Hall-Heroult electrolysis (prebake and Soderberg cells); inert-anode cells.
note: NRCan: 45.0 PJ petroleum coke consumed as anode carbon (non-energetic).

description: Prebake anode baking and Soderberg paste.
note: NRCan: 5.4 PJ.

description: Roasting, flash, continuous and conventional smelting, converting and fire refining for copper, nickel, lead and zinc, and the silicothermic retort for magnesium.
Cryogenic and adsorption air separation supplying oxygen enrichment to flash and bath smelting and to converting.
note: Moved out of the cross-sector air-separation end use (2026-09-14). Oxygen enrichment is what sets smelter fuel use, so it belongs with the smelter.

description: Submerged-arc and electric smelting furnaces for silicon metal, ferrosilicon and other ferroalloys, and titanium slag from ilmenite.
note: Ferroglobe Becancour runs two 24 MW and one 32 MW furnaces for silicon metal and ferrosilicon. Rio Tinto Fer et Titane (Sorel-Tracy) has capacity for about 1.35 Mt/yr of titanium slag. NAICS codes ferroalloys to 331110 (iron and steel); they sit here on the user's decision because the energy use is electric smelting, not steelmaking. Rio Tinto Fer et Titane co-produces about 1 Mt/yr of pig iron; all of the furnace energy and the reductant CO2 stay with the slag and the iron is taken as a co-product carrying none, because one furnace makes both and no allocation basis exists. The pig iron appears on the demand side as foundry feed (other-industry/metal-melting-and-heat-treatment).

description: Leaching, solvent extraction, electrowinning and electrorefining, and molten-salt electrolysis (magnesium cells).
Secondary aluminum, melt and cast shops, holding and reheating furnaces, homogenizing, hot and cold rolling, extrusion.
note: NRCan: aluminum reheating furnaces 2.7 PJ. Semi-fabrication is about 20% of US aluminum energy (hot rolling 10.1%, extrusion 5.3%, cold rolling 4.7%; DOE 2017 aluminum bandwidth study). Canada is mostly primary smelting, so it is folded in here rather than given its own end use.

description: Foundry melting, forging, heat treating and annealing in fabricated metals, machinery and transport equipment.
Textile drying and finishing, paint curing, plastics and rubber moulding and extrusion, other product drying.
note: Most of other industry's energy sits in the cross-sector end uses (CIMS Light Industrial: Heat, Water Heating, Steam, Motive Power, HVAC, Lighting; construction diesel in mobile-equipment).

description: Lumber dry kilns, veneer and strand dryers, hot presses for plywood, OSB and MDF, wood pellet drying.
note: Wood products are 2.9% of Canadian manufacturing energy, the same share as cement (NRCan Trends 2017). Sawing and planing are machine drive. NREL's temperatures come from one SIC and are likely high for lumber kilns; no held source gives kiln temperatures.
